questions.q: What is the central distinction this lesson calls 'the single most important distinction in the entire course'?
options: Classical computers can never represent quantum states, so comparison is meaningless
Only VQE, not QAOA, has ever been proven to have any speedup
A mathematical proof of better asymptotic scaling is not the same claim as a demonstrated practical advantage on real problems today
QAOA and VQE are fundamentally different algorithms with no shared structure
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that a proven scaling result (like amplitude estimation's 1/epsilon) is a separate claim from 'this currently runs faster than the best classical alternative on real problems' -- keeping these distinct is the core professional skill being taught.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why is qubit count described as the 'load-bearing limitation' across every quantum finance application in this chapter?
options: Because only VQE requires qubits; QAOA and amplitude estimation run entirely on classical hardware

Because portfolio QUBOs, amplitude estimation oracles, and VQE molecular Hamiltonians all need qubit counts that scale into the thousands or more for realistic problem sizes, while current hardware tops out in the tens to low hundreds, mostly noisy
Because qubit count has no actual effect on any of these applications
Because current hardware already has millions of usable, error-corrected qubits
questions.explain: The same bottleneck -- insufficient usable qubits relative to realistic problem scale -- recurs across portfolio optimization, amplitude estimation, and VQE, which is why the lesson identifies it as the single most load-bearing constraint.

questions.q: What four questions does the lesson's framework recommend asking about any quantum finance claim?
options: How much did the quantum computer cost; who funded the research; how many authors wrote the paper; what journal published it?
Is the speedup theoretical or empirical; what problem size was tested and is it realistic; was the classical baseline strong or weak; was it run on a simulator or real noisy hardware?
Is the claim written in a press release; does it use the word 'quantum'; is it shorter than 100 words; does it mention finance?
Does the claim mention qubits; does it mention Hamiltonians; does it mention Hartree units; does it mention Pauli operators?
questions.explain: The four-question framework is: theoretical vs. empirical speedup, realistic vs. toy problem size, comparison against a strong vs. weak classical baseline, and simulator vs. real hardware -- these are the questions that distinguish a credible claim from an overstated one.

questions.q: What does the lesson say 'quantum Monte Carlo' changes about a financial risk-estimation pipeline, as a reminder from Lesson 17?
options: It eliminates the need for any model of portfolio returns
Only the sampling/estimation step is potentially accelerated; the underlying probabilistic model of market behavior is unchanged
It has nothing to do with amplitude estimation at all
It replaces the financial model entirely with a quantum-mechanical model of markets
questions.explain: Consistent with Lesson 17, the lesson reiterates that 'quantum Monte Carlo' in this context only concerns accelerating the estimation step -- it is not a more sophisticated model of markets, just a potentially faster way to query the same one.

questions.q: What is the honest, current empirical answer -- according to this lesson -- to whether quantum methods have outperformed strong classical methods on any industrially-sized finance problem?
options: Not yet demonstrated at practically relevant scale, across every application examined in this chapter
The question has never been investigated by anyone in the field
Yes, but only for amplitude estimation, not for QAOA or VQE
Yes, convincingly demonstrated for portfolio optimization with thousands of assets
questions.explain: The lesson states plainly that as of today, the empirical answer across portfolio QUBOs, amplitude estimation, quantum Monte Carlo, and QAOA/VQE generally is 'not yet demonstrated at practically relevant scale' -- the consistent honest-benchmarking stance of the whole course.
